item.title: How to minimize Wi-Fi roaming interruptions for autonomous mobile robots
item.dc:creator: Mikko Niemi
item.description:
Dedicated Wi-Fi scan architectures can improve robot mobility, reliability, and performance, says Synaptics.

The post How to minimize Wi-Fi roaming interruptions for autonomous mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Wi-Fi connectivity needs to be reliable for real-time mobile robot management. Source: Synaptics

An autonomous mobile robot or AMR may cross dozens of Wi-Fi coverage zones during a single shift. Each transition creates a small but potentially consequential communications problem: How does the robot find its next access point without interrupting the connection it is already using?

The answer matters because AMRs, industrial inspection robots, warehouse automation, and healthcare service robots increasingly depend on continuous connectivity for sensor data, telemetry, and control.

In a conventional Wi-Fi architecture, the primary communication radio must periodically stop transmitting and receiving application traffic while it searches for alternative access points. That creates a tradeoff among connectivity, latency, power consumption, and roaming performance.

A dedicated scan architecture separates network discovery from application traffic. The robot can monitor its wireless environment continuously while the primary radio maintains the active connection.

One implementation, Synaptics Scan Core, uses a low-power wireless subsystem to monitor neighboring access points while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. This separation can support faster roaming decisions, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and more efficient scanning.

As robots become more mobile, roaming is mission-critical

Robots are becoming more connected and autonomous across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and service environments. As they move through larger and more complex facilities, reliable wireless connectivity and fast roaming become core design requirements rather than secondary networking considerations.

Unlike stationary Wi-Fi devices, robots move continually between coverage areas while maintaining video, AI inference, telemetry, and fleet-management communications. These combined demands make mobile robotics a strong use case for dedicated scanning architectures.

Modern robots also support increasingly demanding wireless workloads, including HD and multi-camera video, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), AI-assisted navigation, predictive maintenance, and remote operation.

Wireless connectivity has therefore evolved from a convenience into a critical operational subsystem.

Submit your innovation now!

Mobility poses challenges

A mobile robot must maintain application traffic as it moves between Wi-Fi coverage zones. A warehouse robot may roam dozens or even hundreds of times during a shift. Each roaming event can introduce:

  • Increased latency
  • Packet loss
  • Video disruption
  • Delayed control responses
  • Reduced productivity

Common performance targets for robotics deployments include:

Requirement Typical Target
Roaming latency <80 ms
Sustained throughput 20 Mbps
Packet loss during roaming <2%

For many autonomous systems, meeting these targets is important to safe and efficient operation.

Key requirements and pain points

Although stakeholders evaluate robotics systems differently, several wireless performance measures consistently emerge as critical.

Roaming latency

A typical roaming process includes the following steps:

  1. Network discovery
  2. Candidate evaluation
  3. Authentication
  4. Security key exchange
  5. Reassociation

Each step adds delay. In robotics applications, excessive roaming latency can affect navigation, fleet coordination, teleoperation, and machine-vision performance.

Packet loss

Even brief connectivity interruptions can affect AMR operations and data transfer. Robots often require communications performance that is consistent and predictable enough for real-time operation.

Power consumption

AMRs must continuously balance battery performance and energy efficiency. Aggressive scanning improves roaming responsiveness but typically increases power consumption.

Dense RF environments

Warehouses, factories, airports, and hospitals often contain many access points, multiple wireless protocols, and significant RF reflections. These conditions place additional demands on roaming algorithms.

Dedicated scanning can address mobile robot connectivity

Traditional Wi-Fi clients use the primary communication radio for both application traffic and network discovery. During a background scan, the radio temporarily leaves its serving channel to look for neighboring access points, interrupting active traffic and potentially adding delay or packet loss.

A dedicated scan architecture assigns continuous monitoring of the wireless environment to a separate low-power resource. The primary Wi-Fi radio can remain focused on application traffic while candidate access points are identified in advance.

Source: Synaptics

Synaptics Scan Core is one implementation of this general architectural approach. A dedicated scan resource removes this contention between active communications and network discovery.

Source: Synaptics

Traditional Wi-Fi versus Scan Core

Conventional Wi-Fi Dedicated Scan Core
Main communication radio performs scanning Dedicated Scan Core performs scanning
User traffic interrupted during scans User traffic radio is not interrupted by scan operations
Reactive roaming Proactive roaming
Higher scan power Lower scan power
Longer roaming time Faster roaming
Periodic access point discovery Continuous AP discovery

Key benefits

  • Continuous network awareness: The scan radio continuously monitors neighboring channels while the primary radio remains connected.
  • Faster roaming decisions: Candidate access points are discovered before signal quality degrades.
  • Lower packet loss: Active communications continue during background scanning.
  • More predictable performance: Roaming behavior becomes more consistent and predictable.
  • Improved power efficiency: Background scanning can be optimized without disrupting active communications.

Instead of waiting for connectivity to deteriorate, the wireless subsystem can prepare for the next roaming event while application traffic continues on the primary radio.

Measured Scan Core benefits

Synaptics said its platform characterization measured substantial improvements in scanning efficiency:

Metric Improvement
Scan time Up to 65% faster
Overall scan duration Approximately 40% shorter
Scan power Up to 75% lower
Scan current Up to 77% lower

Source: Synaptics robotics platform characterization

In a mobile robot, these improvements can contribute to faster roaming, lower scan energy, longer battery life, and steadier application traffic. Actual results will depend on the platform, network topology, traffic load, and RF environment.

Applying dedicated scanning to mobile robots

Commercial connectivity platforms are beginning to incorporate dedicated scanning. For instance, Synaptics offers an integrated platform combining Wi-Fi 7, dual Bluetooth 6.0, and IEEE 802.15.4, as well as multi-band operation across 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz.

Within that platform, Scan Core provides a dedicated scan resource that operates independently of the primary WLAN subsystem. This allows scanning and active communications to occur simultaneously rather than compete for the same radio.

Multi-band awareness

The platform evaluates candidate access points across multiple frequency bands, helping the robot maintain connectivity as it moves through a facility.

Fast channel switching

The architecture supports rapid transitions between the main and scan resources. On the Synaptics robotics validation platform, switching between resources was measured on the order of microseconds.

Roaming test results

Figure 3 summarizes the minimum and maximum measured roaming times across three representative scenarios. In Synaptics platform testing, all results remained below the 80 ms target while continuous 20 Mbps UDP traffic was maintained:

Source: Synaptics

Wireless mobility becomes part of robot performance

As AMRs take on more complex workloads and operate across larger, denser environments, wireless mobility becomes part of the robot’s performance envelope. Roaming affects productivity, fleet efficiency, the user experience, and, in some applications, safe operation.

Conventional Wi-Fi makes the communication radio divide its time between application traffic and network discovery. A dedicated scan architecture separates those functions, allowing the robot to identify its next connection without interrupting the one it is already using.

Dedicated scanning and Wi-Fi 7 enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio (eMLSR) address different parts of wireless mobility. Dedicated scanning improves awareness of nearby access points; eMLSR improves how the device uses multiple links. Together, they can make roaming faster and more predictable without forcing designers to trade application performance against network awareness.

In Synaptics internal validation, eMLSR delivered up to a 10x latency improvement over single-link operation under congested conditions. Results vary with network topology, traffic load, and RF conditions. eMLSR can provide many multi-link operation latency benefits without requiring multiple fully active radios.

Synaptics says Scan Core can help mobile robots maintain coverage. Source: Synaptics

Glossary

Autonomous mobile robot An AMR can navigating and performing tasks using sensors, AI, and wireless connectivity without requiring fixed guidance infrastructure or direct human control.
Access point An AP is a wireless networking device that provides Wi-Fi connectivity to client devices within a coverage area.
Enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio eMLSR is a Wi-Fi 7 capability that enables a single radio to intelligently utilize multiple wireless links, improving latency, reliability, and power efficiency.
Fleet management Software and network infrastructure used to monitor, coordinate, and manage multiple AMRs operating within the same environment.
Latency The time required for data to travel between devices. Low and predictable latency is critical for real-time robotics applications.
Multi-Link Operation MLO is a Wi-Fi 7 feature that allows communication over multiple wireless links, improving throughput, reliability, and network efficiency.
Packet loss Data packets that fail to reach their destination. Excessive packet loss can interrupt video, telemetry, and real-time control.
Roaming The process by which a Wi-Fi client transitions from one access point to another while maintaining network connectivity.
Scan Core A dedicated low-power wireless receive subsystem that continuously monitors the wireless environment while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. By separating network awareness from communications, Scan Core enables faster roaming, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and improved power efficiency, according to Synaptics.
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping SLAM is a navigation technique that enables a robot to build a map of its environment while simultaneously determining its own position within that map.
Simultaneous Transmit and Receive STR is a Wi-Fi 7 Multi-Link Operation mode that enables simultaneous transmission and reception over multiple wireless links, maximizing throughput and reducing latency.
User Datagram Protocol UDP is a lightweight transport protocol used for real-time applications such as video streaming, voice, gaming, and telemetry. Unlike TCP, UDP does not retransmit lost packets, making it well suited for measuring network latency, packet loss, and roaming performance in wireless systems.
Wi-Fi 7  The latest generation of Wi-Fi technology (IEEE 802.11be) introduced features such as MLO, wider channel bandwidths, lower latency, and improved efficiency in dense wireless environments.

About the author

Mikko Niemi is a product manager for wireless products at Synaptics Inc. He has more than 15 years of experience across industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), semiconductor, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) sectors. Niemi specializes in building and scaling intelligent, data-driven platforms that power connected infrastructure, smart energy systems, and next-generation industrial applications.

He previously worked at Lantronix, where he led a portfolio that included industrial IoT gateways, cloud-based, SaaS device management platforms, and global connectivity services—delivering edge-to-cloud systems that integrate real-time telemetry, AI/machine learning analytics, and robust security at scale. Niemi previosly held management roles at Silicon Labs and Landis+Gyr. He holds an MBA and a Master’s in electronics engineering.

item.title: ARM Institute consortium grows to more than 500 organizations
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The ARM Institute reached the milestone as it prepares to host its 10th annual member meeting in Pittsburgh.

The post ARM Institute consortium grows to more than 500 organizations appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The annual ARM Institute member meeting takes place in Pittsburgh. Source: ARM Institute

The Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing, or ARM Institute last week said that that its member consortium has grown to include more than 500 organizations nationwide, with thousands of individual subject matter experts represented within these organizations. The organization collaborates with its consortium and the U.S. government to promote the U.S. as leading nation in manufacturing output through the adoption of robotics and AI.

“We are proud to work with our consortium to build a resilient, secure, and bright future for U.S. manufacturing,” stated Jorgen Pedersen, CEO of the ARM Institute. “Our member consortium is the foundation of our Institute and integral to our mission.”

“Our members have collaborated with us on hundreds of technology projects, helped us launch major initiatives, including our national workforce resource RoboticsCareer.org, supported manufacturers through their robotics and automation journey, and more,” he added. “We look forward to celebrating this milestone at our 10th Annual Member Meeting later this month.”

Founded in 2017, the ARM Institute is a Manufacturing Innovation Institute (MII) funded by the Office of the Secretary of War under Agreement No. W911NF-17-3-0004 and is part of the Manufacturing USA network. The organization relies on its member consortium and partners across industry, academia, and government to promote U.S. manufacturing leadership through the adoption of robotics and AI.

ARM Institute conducts activities with and for members

The ARM Institute said it focuses on catalyzing innovative yet practical robotics and physical AI solutions. The Pittsburg-based institute said it is also working to grow and prepare the U.S. workforce for advanced manufacturing careers.

“The ARM Institute’s member consortium is expansive, bridging gaps and bringing varied perspectives together to catalyze robotics, physical AI, and workforce solutions to strengthen U.S. manufacturing,” stated the organization.

Last month, the institute issued a project call from the U.S. Navy to address needs in the shipbuilding industrial base. This month, the ARM Institute put out a request for proposals for a skills gap analysis for a localized talent supply chain to support the organic and defense industrial base.

Its consortium members include manufacturers of all sizes, defense contractors, technology providers offering robotics and AI systems, research universities, community colleges, vocational schools, government entities, startups, and others.

ARM Institute membership is at the organizational level and provides access to funding opportunities, member-exclusive events, a digital member community for virtual collaboration, and more. Companies, governmental bodies, and educational institutions that otherwise would be considered competitors work together through the institute for the benefit of the nation and manufacturers across the U.S., asserted the organization.

10th annual member meeting coming soon

The ARM Institute marked the membership milestone as it prepares to host its 10th Annual Member Meeting from Nov. 17 to 19. This member-exclusive event convenes experts from across ARM’s consortium and the U.S. government for two and a half days of networking, collaboration, and knowledge-sharing.

The event in Pittsburgh will feature expert-led presentations, networking and curated matchmaking, a Member Showcase Hall, and more. This year’s event will feature celebratory content and activities in recognition of the anniversary.

Registration for the ARM Institute’s 2026 Annual Member Meeting closes on Nov. 13. Register or join the ARM Member Consortium before then to gain access to the meeting.

item.title: Robot integration brings high-precision production to midmarket manufacturers
item.dc:creator: Lou Farrell
item.description:
Properly integrated industrial and collaborative robots can help midmarket manufacturers, according to a columnist.

The post Robot integration brings high-precision production to midmarket manufacturers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
High-precision manufacturing was once considered something exclusive to large corporations. However, advances in robotic integration and automated manufacturing have changed this perception.

Sophisticated capabilities are becoming accessible to midmarket and smaller operations. This shift has led to a more even competitive landscape.

Smaller manufacturers have an opportunity to reach new levels of accuracy and efficiency. Today’s robotic systems can help these producers modernize targeted workflows without overhauling their entire production operations.

Robotic innovations drive efficiency for manufacturers

The evolution of robotics has led to more democratized precision manufacturing processes. This is evident across industrial robots and agile collaborative robots.

Key benefits of these innovations can include:

  • Cost and footprint: The potential for lower investment costs and compact designs can make robotic systems economically viable. It can also simplify integration into existing layouts.
  • Enhanced programming: Intuitive interfaces and lead-through teaching methods support quick deployment and reconfiguration. This reduces the training typically required for operators without robotics expertise.
  • Sensors and AI-driven capabilities: Sensors, such as vision systems and force-torque sensors, can be integrated with AI. This enables robots to understand, react and adapt with precision.
  • Safety and collaboration: Cobots can work safely alongside humans without extensive guarding. This fosters a flexible human-robot workforce that combines optimal utilization and human dexterity.

These advancements mean that midmarket manufacturers can overcome hurdles like skilled labor shortages, rising costs, and quality demands.

Submit your innovation now!

Real-world impact of robotic integration for precision manufacturers

Here are some use cases that show how a diverse range of manufacturers have taken advantage of recent advances in robotics.

1. SCHUNK R-C2 automation for flexible production

Torneria Novoletto is an Italian organization specializing in sophisticated components for the chemical, medical, and pharmaceutical sectors.

The company faced obstacles in achieving high precision and process reliability for medium-sized batches. It implemented SCHUNK’s R-C2 automation concept, integrating advanced clamping devices and grippers with robotic handling.

Introducing this system helped to support high operational flexibility. Setup and changeover times were also significantly reduced because the SCHUNK R-C2 allows the continuous handling of workpiece sizes and automated reclamping.

This innovative robotic integration has helped Torneria Novoletto to pursue an unmanned 24/7 operation, increase machine utilization, and mitigate shortages of skilled labor.

Torneria Novoletto shows the compact efficiency of the R-C2 automation. Source: SCHUNK

2. Cobot integration for part marking

Telesis, a leading provider of industrial marking solutions, integrated its part marking technology with systems from Universal Robots.

The company offers advanced laser and dot peen markers. When a Telesis laser marking system is integrated with a UR force- and power-limited robot arm, it creates a precise and flexible method of identifying automated parts.

Innovations like this ensure that systems can be safely deployed alongside human workers. Robotic integrations have provided Telesis with a streamlined marking process without complex safety enclosures, consistent high-quality marking on various materials and part geometries, and added traceability and quality control.

Telesis demonstrates integrated laser-marking systems with robotic control. Source: Universal Robots

3. FANUC M-20 robots enhance throughput and scale

Northern Kentucky Machine (NKM), a flexible job shop, experienced labor shortages and production capacity challenges. Its strategic response included the use of automated manufacturing solutions, such as deploying FANUC M-20 Series industrial robots.

By using Automation Within Reach’s (AWR) “RC-2” CNC machine-tending system, the integration increased NKM’s throughput and machine utilization.

Operators quickly adapted to programming and running these robotic cells. This helped to enable “lights-out” manufacturing for longer runs, freeing up human workers for other tasks.

The FANUC robots have provided NKM with the scalability needed to pursue and take on larger projects, deliver consistent part quality, drive growth, and compete with other midsize organizations.

NKM used the M-20 Series robot to boost the efficiency of human workers. Source: FANUC

4. ActiNav enables bin picking and legacy equipment extension

PrecisionForm Inc. is a producer of small custom metal parts. It faced the challenge of automating bin picking for CNC machines.

By deploying Universal Robots’ ActiNav system, PrecisionForm integrated a UR5 cobot with advanced vision and path-planning capabilities. This approach led to reliable part picking from deep bins that were then loaded into CNC machines.

Challenging geometries were less of an issue, and operators were freed up to manage multiple machines. The UR cobots helped reduce labor challenges and extend the lifespan of older CNC equipment.

By adding a relatively inexpensive robotic solution, PrecisionForm Inc gained additional utility from existing machinery, increased the potential return on investment (ROI) as a midmarket operation, and improved daily production.

Uses can easily deploy and calibrate the ActiNav system, says UR. Source: Universal Robots

Capabilities evolve for midmarket manufacturers

The accessibility of precision manufacturing marks a crucial moment for many industries. Robotic integration is no longer exclusive to the world’s largest enterprises.

Innovations offering ultra-high accuracy and consistent quality are now economically and operationally viable for midsized manufacturers. The benefits that organizations such as Telesis, Torneria Novoletto, NKM, and PrecisionForm now have shown that modern robotics can drive sustainable growth.

Robotic solutions continue to evolve. As they do, the advantages of automated manufacturing will grow alongside those changes. With thoughtful and careful implementation, a new generation of agile and highly precise manufacturers will be waiting to reap the benefits of this exciting new world.

About the author

Lou Farrell, a senior editor at Revolutionized, has written on the topics of robotics, computing, and technology for years. He has a great passion for the stories he covers and for writing in general.

This article is posted with permission.

item.title: Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Brian Donnelly, the VP and GM of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, said the new version of Stretch has been in the works for two and a half years. 

The post Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The new Stretch features an updated modular design that enables “plug and play” part swaps. | Source: Boston Dynamics

Boston Dynamics Inc. this week unveiled Stretch Gen 2, the latest generation of its autonomous mobile trailer unloading robot. With over 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes handled under its belt, the company built the updated robot to maximize uptime and streamline maintenance.

Brian Donnelly, the vice president and general manager of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, told The Robot Report that the company has been working on the new version of Stretch for around two and a half years.

“When we made the first generation of Stretch, we were focused on trying to get a product out into the market as fast as possible and really get it in customers’ hands and get it operational,” he said. “It was not the easiest to manufacture; there were a lot of components.”

“[With Stretch 2], we really were focused on simplification, hardening the robot, and really driving improved reliability and performance,” added Donnelly. “That’s really what drove a lot of our decisions was just making the robot better in every way.”

Stretch Gen 2 can unload up to 1,000 cases per hour. This rate is highly dependent on factors such as case weight and how neat or disorderly cases are stacked. It has a multipick feature, a battery that can last two shifts, and a fast charger that can get it to 90% charge in about 75 minutes.

The mobile manipulator also features onboard lighting, making it easier to work in dark trailers, and a pre-trained vision system that can detect most packages without programming needed.

Stretch’s hardware upgrades improve durability

Boston Dynamics geared many of Stretch Gen 2’s upgrades towards reducing downtime and making the robot more durable. For example, the Waltham, Mass.-based company also cut 81% of the internal cabling, around half a mile’s worth.

“[Cabling] is weight, it’s cost, and its points of failure, particularly when you have something that’s in constant motion, you’re creating strain on those cables with every motion,” Donnelly said. “If you don’t have good strain relief, you don’t have good ways of managing the cables in the robot. It can cause stress on the cables and then failure.”

Donnelly said Hyundai helped the company source a cable harness through its automotive supply chain. This isn’t the only thing Boston Dynamics learned from the automotive industry. Stretch Gen 2 uses heavy-duty automotive-grade connectors. These hold up to the vibration of rapid, high-torque box handling and driving over uneven floors.

“In the automotive industry, they have to deal with a lot of real-world challenges in their vehicles. There’s a lot of miles driven dealing with shock and vibration and things like this,” Donnelly said. “As a robot moves around the world, just like a car, if you don’t have latching connectors, then they can sort of wiggle apart. By leveraging those automotive connectors, we’re much more confident that the connectors are going to stay latched together and not pull apart in the field.”

The robot also has continuous rotation joints that move beyond 360° so they no longer hit hard stops. This can help prevent previously caused mechanical stress. Donnelly pointed out this also makes the robot more productive, as it can completely optimize its trajectory planning and move in any direction.

The emergency stop on the robot now sits lower and is recessed. Boston Dynamics made the exterior panels with new materials so a falling box is far less likely to trip an unintentional safety stoppage or break a panel.

How Stretch Gen 2 gets a grip on multiple boxes

The gripper is the part of the robot that often deals with the most stress. It’s making contact with all of the the things the robot needs to handle. Stretch Gen 2 features an upgraded gripper with new valve systems and more precise sensing improves grasping and placement to optimize fast-paced picks.

“[The new gripper] has a valve in every suction cup, which enables us to pick multiple boxes with a single motion of the arm, which substantially increases our throughput,” Donnelly explained. “If we can pick multiple boxes, with a single motion of the arm, we get much higher throughput because the pick cycle of picking up a box from the floor of a container and place it to a conveyor is dominated by arm movement. So, if we can keep the arm moving and just do more every cycle, that is really effective and improves the rate at which we can unload a truck for our customers.”

The new gripper is also better at configuring boxes on the conveyor belt in ways that work best for Boston Dynamics’ customers, and use less power in picking up boxes.

“Every cup is individually sensed and actuated, so we know when we have good suction,” said Donnelly. “We only have the valve open to pull suction when we have good contact on a box, so that enables us to reduce the amount of power we’re spending running on the vacuum pump, so we’re not pulling suction through cups that don’t have good contact. It also enables us to, when we pick up those multiple boxes, singulate them onto the conveyor.”

Stretch Gen 2 brings service time down to just hours

With Stretch Gen 2, Boston Dynamics didn’t just want to reduce the frequency of service calls; it also wanted to make those service calls faster when they do happen.

“We didn’t have as much experience from a serviceability perspective as a company when we made the first-generation robot,” Donnelly said. “We’ve since deployed these robots, serviced them in the field, and hired a lot of people who have a lot more experience than we originally did in service. Their input and guidance really helped us to make a robot that’s much more manufacturable and more serviceable.”

The robot doesn’t require dynamic cables and complex harnesses. Instead it uses standardized high-strength fasteners to cut down on tool changes and hands-on repair time. For example, the company can perform a full swerve drive swap in just one hour. Before, this process could take an entire day.

Stretch Gen 2 also features new onboard diagnostics and maintenance tools. These put more routine service in the hands of a customer’s own maintenance team, so robots stay on the dock with less reliance on outside support.

Updated robot continuously improves its performance

The new robot runs on a redesigned onboard computing platform that is constantly improving. Boston Dynamics said it will regularly release software updates to bring gains in case detection, motion planning, pick strategies, and world modeling across an entire fleet, with no hardware changes required.

Donnelly said that with the company’s most recent update, it saw a 24% increase in unload rate across its fleet of fielded robots.

“A lot of our activity on this program is really focused on the software. We’re constantly improving our computer vision capabilities to be able to better perceive boxes and conveyors and container walls, and then really pick boxes and place them to convey more and more productivity over time,” Donnelly said.

Right now, Donnelly said Boston Dynamics releases new software, on average, on a monthly basis.

Submit your innovation now!

How have customers reacted to Gen 2 so far?

Donnelly said Boston Dynamics already has Stretch Gen 2 running at multiple customer sites.

“Customers are really happy with it, and they’re continuing to rely on it to do its work every day,” said Donnelly. “We’re going into these existing sites and deploying these robots within two weeks. The folks who are taking over operating the robots are the folks who are otherwise doing repetitive heavy lifting of these boxes and containers.”

“We put a lot of effort into ensuring that the user experience, from an operator perspective, is really simple. It doesn’t require a ton of training,” he added. “A person can drive the robot into a container, step out of the safety work cell, and they press a big Play button, and then the robot does the rest.”

Many of the people working with Stretch used to spend their days unloading heavy boxes from trailers.

“Fundamentally, unloading trailers is one of the worst jobs in the warehouse,” Donnelly said. “It can be really hot in a container that’s been sitting in a yard in the summer. It can be super cold in the winter. Then the work itself is moving heavy boxes repeatedly from down low or up high. It puts a lot of strain and stress on people’s bodies.”

item.title: Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank acquisition of ABB Robotics
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
China's prohibition of SoftBank's purchase of ABB Robotics reflects wider concerns about data and AI, say experts.

The post Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank acquisition of ABB Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
ABB Robotics has integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into RobotStudio. Source: ABB Robotics

Yesterday, ABB Robotics confirmed to The Robot Report that China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has blocked SoftBank Group Corp.’s planned acquisition of ABB Robotics. Regulators had expressed concern that data for training artificial intelligence models could be transferred overseas.

ABB Robotics is already a significant manufacturer and provider of robotics in China. The Zurich-based company stated that it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.”

Other countries are moving to protect what they view as sovereign physical AI. For instance, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) recently banned new models of certain connected advanced devices, including legged robots and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Companies such as Intel and Husqvarna have already received conditional approvals.

In addition, the U.S. Department of Commerce last week determined that imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and related components pose a threat to the U.S. economy and national security. This could lead to tariffs.

Government investigations can directly affect major robotics and AI companies. European antitrust scrutiny of Amazon’s proposed acquisition of iRobot was one reason why that deal was terminated, with iRobot subsequently entering bankruptcy proceedings. The robotic vacuum pioneer has since been picked up by Shenzhen, China-based Picea Robotics Co.

ABB Robotics as focused on automation and AI

ABB Robotics claimed that it is the only company whose integrated portfolio includes industrial automation, software, force- and power-limited cobots, and AMRs. The company said its “autonomous versatile robotics” help businesses of all sizes in industries including automotive, electronics, and logistics.

ABB Robotics has installed more than 500,000 robots around the world and employs about 7,000 people. Its U.S. headquarters are in Auburn Hills, Mich. In October 2025, parent company ABB said it had agreed to sell its robotics division to Japan-based SoftBank Group Corp. for $5.3 billion.

“Considering the intensive competition in traditional robotics, established manufacturers like ABB will need to lead the charge in AI-driven robotics to protect their margins,” said Samantha Mou, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis. “However, achieving this will require significant investment. The substantial long-term R&D costs may be a key factor behind ABB’s decision to sell its robotics business.”

“Compared with the other Big 4 vendors [FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa], ABB was already quick in combining AI with its products, which is an area where it can have synergy with SoftBank,” Mou told The Robot Report. She said that companies in Europe, Asia, and the Americas are hoping that AI, which has already been used for ease of programming, monitoring, and predictive maintenance, can be generalized to more processes.

“AI gives ABB Robotics considerable potential,” said Robert Little, a business development advisor and former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc, on LinkedIn. “But turning that potential into commercially useful systems requires sustained investment. In my humble opinion, backing that investment within ABB becomes a harder decision when robotics has to compete for funding against higher-margin businesses. ABB also saw limited synergies between robotics and the rest of the company.”

“SoftBank made sense,” he added. “ABB brings robot manufacturing, application expertise and established customer relationships. SoftBank could bring additional investment and a clear focus on AI.”

Sovereign physical AI becomes a strategic concern

“Post Astra, robotics data has become more strategic,” posted Financial Times reporter Zijing Wu, in reference to the GPT-6 model that OpenAI released in September and that Chinese AI firms used to train their models.

“The NDRC [China’s National Development and Reform Commission] had been concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas, where it could be used to train AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, in which SoftBank is a major investor, sources say,” said Wu on X.

Countries have become increasingly aware of the competitive advantage promised by the convergence of automation and AI.

“What makes this particularly significant is that industrial robotics is increasingly being viewed not simply as manufacturing equipment, but as strategically important technology at the intersection of automation, data, and AI,” Ash Sharma, managing director of Interact Analysis, told The Robot Report.

“China is a critical market for ABB Robotics, so separating the Chinese operation from a global transaction of this scale would be extremely challenging,” he added. “More broadly, this highlights how robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capability are becoming important considerations in cross-border M&A as physical AI develops.”

Ahmed Humayun, head of go to market for defense manufacturing at Gecko Robotics, posted to LinkedIn: “This move reflects Chinese concerns about asset transfers to Japan during a time of heightened Chinese-Japanese tension, but [it] also shows concerns about robotics data generated in China being transferred abroad to train foundation models. The most recent example of China flexing its economic muscle and demonstrating that it has many levers to prevent intellectual property and assets from leaving its soil — even when developed by foreign companies.”

“I was worried this might happen,” said Little. “Over the years, I have seen ABB‘s strength in China grow. Where do we go from here?”

“My take: ABB has built a strong presence in China, but heavily subsidized Chinese robot makers are becoming stronger competitors at home and expanding into Europe,” he wrote. “That creates more pressure on pricing and margins that were not that great to begin with fall even further.”

“There may still be negotiations that find a way forward,” concluded Little. “For now, ABB is in a pickle.”

item.title: How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market?
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Humanoid developer Agility Robotics ended its first day of trading on the Nasdaq just 2% above where it started, at $11.49.

The post How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market? appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Agility says its Digit 5 humanoids can lift up to 50 lb. | Source: Agility Robotics

Earlier today, Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker “AGLT.” The company claimed that it is “the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public.”

Agility started the day trading at $11.26 per share, above the initial $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. It was a day of ups and downs, as it was for many tech stocks. It hit its lowest price at $8.40, and its highest at $12.15.

The company ended up closing the day trading slightly above (2%) where it had started, at $11.49. Other pure-play robotics providers did not fare so well.

Serve Robotics, another publicly traded robotics company that offers sidewalk delivery robots, ended down 12.45%. Surgical robotics leader Intuitive Surgical ended down 2.82%. Symbotic, which provides end-to-end warehouse automation, ended down 2.47%. In addition, PROCEPT BioRobotics Corp., which provides robotic aquablation therapy, ended down 6.42%.

While Unitree, another humanoid robotics provider, doesn’t trade on the Nasdaq, it is public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s STR Market. It’s one of the only other publicly traded humanoid robot providers.

Unitree first debuted on the market at 150.80 yuan ($22.55 U.S.), and saw some quick success, hitting a high of 1,100 yuan ($164.46) that day. Just a few weeks after debuting on the market, it was down almost 53% from its first-day high. The company is still working to climb back up to those numbers.

In addition, China has reportedly tightened its own requirements for initial public offerings for humanoid robot startups.

Technology and AI-related stocks struggle across markets

Note that the entire Nasdaq is down 5.52% today, which means Agility was beating this overall trend. Much of these losses were concentrated in AI-related stocks.

NVIDIA ended the day down 9.26% from its opening price. AMD ended down 17.26%, while Qualcomm dropped 9.49%. Microsoft was down 3.58%. Rockwell Automation was down 14.15%.

Other markets have had some of their worst days since April 2025. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 3.44%.

This week’s midterm elections have caused the markets to fluctuate. While they saw some sharp gains yesterday, many of those gains dissipated today. Today’s losses have a lot to do with investor uncertainty around future data center buildouts with a now Democratically controlled Senate and House.

What comes next for Agility Robotics

From left to right, Cassie and Digit through the years. | Source: Agility Robotics

The Robot Report will be watching Agility’s performance on the markets in the coming months. Already, the company alluded to adding more robots to its portfolio. The Robot Report also broke the news about Agility exploring wheel-based robots in September 2026.

Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, talked more about this plan in a recent video. In the video, she mentioned the possible addition of a smaller bipedal form factor to the company’s lineup.

Agility claimed that for its newest Digit 5, it has more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders, subject to contractual milestones and product specifications. It expects to begin Digit 5 deliveries to early-access customers in 2027.

Agility’s public offering, which it conducted after completing a merger with special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp XI, will provide around $465 million in gross proceeds before expenses.

item.title: How Ambi Robotics helps its customers prepare for peak season
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Ambi Robotics' co-founder and COO Stephen McKinley says the company is installing eight new systems at customer sites before peak season.

The post How Ambi Robotics helps its customers prepare for peak season appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The AmbiSort B Series can streamline final-mile deliver operations with automated induction, scanning, and ‘end-to-end’ sortation. | Source: Ambi Robotics

As Black Friday and the start of peak season draw near, logistics providers across the country are getting ready for the rush. Each year, these providers could see a 25% to 40% increase in throughput, according to Stephen McKinley, co-founder and chief operating officer at Ambi Robotics.

This year, Ambi is expecting its customers to experience a 9% to 10% increase compared with peak season last year.

“Despite anything that might be going on in the economy, volume continues to ramp and e-commerce spending remains high,” McKinley told The Robot Report. “That puts familiar pressures on our clients to perform in all of their individual sites, and we’re feeling that pressure also, because our systems are core to their functions.”

For Ambi, preparing for the season means installing new systems at eight facilities before peak season starts.

“Most of those new sites are with this new version of AmbiSort, and though that’s not a new product, it’s definitely a new variation,” said McKinley. “We’re excited about supporting that through peak season, and we want to make sure that goes perfectly, of course, for our customers.”

The Berkeley, Calif.-based company is also working to ensure that its team members will be readily available for logistics customers when they need them.

“We move into a more reactive state of being, where we’ll have about half of the team traveling around to different sites to check in with what’s going on, and the other half of the team is ready to jump to solve issues as they come up,” McKinley said.

How to increase throughput without adding new systems

While some of Ambi Robotics’ customers plan to have more systems go live for peak season, there are other ways to increase throughput, McKinley said.

“[Customers] will often add more shifts into existing operations or bring on more people to be working alongside our systems, so we can help with training,” he noted. “We offer more training to customers right before peak season to make sure they know how to effectively use the systems.”

Properly training the operators working with robots on a daily basis can make a big difference in how the system performs.

“Over the course of the year, we’re tracking how the systems are performing all the time,” said McKinley. “The performance of the systems is related to the inherent quality of that piece of machinery, which doesn’t really fluctuate, but also related to how the customer interacts with that machine and how attentive they are to it, or how well trained the operators are. So, we can help by stepping in and making sure that everybody knows what to do and has the right mindset when they’re approaching their system.”

Ambi decreases downtime, rolls out incremental improvements

Nobody wants a robot to fail, but they especially don’t want a robot to fail when they need to handle a massive increase in volume. This means reducing downtime is even more important for Ambi Robotics right now. To do this, the company forward-deploys spare parts to different sites.

“Normally, we would have spare inventory here at our headquarters in Berkeley, and we would send things out as needed. That spares inventory is also what we use to pull form to build new systems,” McKinley said. “During peak seasons, we’ll bring in more spares and then deploy those out to specific locations in the East Coast that are hubs of customer activity.”

For example, McKinley said Cincinnati is a central zone for a lot of the Ambi’s installs in the Midwest. “We’ll even go so far as to put spare computers or spare high critical items at each site that will carry more inventory at customer locations during peak season,” he continued.

When it comes to rolling out improvements in its AI systems, Ambi takes a conservative approach.

“We’ve been a physical AI company since 2018 when we started. We know how important it is to have systems out there in the world that are performing at predictable levels. So, we don’t have systems that are self-improving over time,” McKinley said. “As we generate more data from our systems, we’ll use that to retrain our systems and then process that improvement through an A/B test within a controlled environment to see what happens before we roll it out into the rest of the field.”

When customers need help from Ambi, they will always speak with a person

While it’s important to improve the technology, roll out new systems, and add more shifts, McKinley said it’s just as important for Ambi to build trust with its customers.

“The people who will be answering the phones for our support hotline are the people who will go to the facilities and do the training and make the fixes,” he explained. “I think that’s very important, because we’re building a layer of trust with the operators and with the people on site who need to maintain the systems in our absence, and the management who’s on site.”

“When they pick up the phone, they’ll know the voice on the other end, and that person will be familiar with them,” McKinley added. “That’s helped build trust significantly. That trust has been, in my opinion, the most important factor for those large customers to be adopting physical AI in the real world.”

Instead of using AI to directly interact with customers, Ambi has developed an AI system to help its employees more quickly solve problems for its customers. This AI system also makes it easier for Ambi to onboard new employees, McKinley said.

“We’ve been working on basically collecting all the data from our support tickets and then feeding that into our own AI model to assist in support. We have a very lean, very small team,” he said. “Now, we’ve got these AI assistants that are helping us keep track of performance on sites, then predict when things might be going wrong, and then helping us as a support organization.”

item.title: Chinese regulators block SoftBank’s $5.4B acquisition of ABB Robotics
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Chinese authorities blocked the deal over concerns about robot data being transferred overseas and used to train AI models.

The post Chinese regulators block SoftBank’s $5.4B acquisition of ABB Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
ABB Robotics has about 7,000 employees, and its U.S. headquarters and factory are in Auburn Hills, Mich. | Source: ABB Robotics

It has been more than a year since ABB announced it singed an agreement to sell its robotics division to the Japanese tech giant SoftBank Group. The $5.375 billion deal is now being blocked by Chinese regulators, ABB confirmed to The Robot Report.

China‘s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has prohibited the acquisition in the country. Authorities expressed concerns about robotics data being transferred overseas and used to train AI models, according to The Financial Times, which first reported that the deal was blocked.

You may be wondering why Chinese regulators have so much say in a Japanese company acquiring a Zurich-based industrial automation provider, but China makes up a major portion of ABB’s revenue. For the entire FY 2025, ABB Robotics saw $928,000 in orders from China, an increase from the $662,000 in orders it brought in from China in 2024.

This is a growing region for ABB. In Q3 2026, ABB Robotics saw a 32% increase in business in China alone.

ABB also manufacturers a significant number of robots in its Shanghai factory. About 90% of its machines built for Chinese customers are manufactured locally, employing thousands of people in the country.

Looking ahead, ABB said it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.”

Is the robotics industry becoming a new political battleground?

This news comes as global politics becomes increasingly important in the world of robotics. This isn’t the first time China has blocked an international deal citing national security concerns. In April, the country prevented Meta from acquiring Manus, an AI startup that was founded in China but then relocated to Singapore, for $2 billion.

Here in the U.S., the federal government has taken steps to slow down foreign robot suppliers within the country. Just last week, U.S. President Donald J. Trump said the secretary of commerce had submitted a Section 232 report about the national security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as related parts and components.

The Section 232 statement specifically cited “advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles” as providing direct support to the U.S. military. While it’s unclear right now what this will mean for the robotics industry, it could lead to tariffs on foreign-made robots.

Already, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has banned new foreign-made advanced robotic devices, including mobile robots such as humanoids and quadrupeds. The FCC said these machines could create create supply chain vulnerabilities and pose a cybersecurity risk to American critical infrastructure.

Editor’s note: The Robot Report has reached out to sources for more comment, which we will publish.

item.title: Agility Robotics begins trading on Nasdaq
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
Agility Robotics becomes the first U.S.-based legged humanoid company to be publicly listed.

The post Agility Robotics begins trading on Nasdaq appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market this morning under the ticker “AGLT,” after the company completed its merger with special-purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, Churchill Capital Corp XI.

Agility’s stock opened at $11.26 per share, which was above the $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. The Salem, Ore.-based company‘s stock was at $10.30 as of press time.

“Today marks an important milestone for Agility, but the bigger story is what it means for the future of work,” stated Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility Robotics. “AI is moving beyond the digital world and into the physical world, creating new possibilities for how people and machines work together. At Agility, that future is already taking shape.”

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” she added. “Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together.”

Churchill XI shareholders approved the deal on Nov. 2, with more than 84% of votes cast in favor. The transaction closed on Nov. 4. Shares held by existing Agility shareholders and by the Churchill sponsor will be subject to a lock-up restriction on sales for 180 days after the 6ransaction closes, subject to early release based on certain stock price performance measures.

The deal provides with about $465 million in gross proceeds before expenses. That includes about $164 million from Churchill XI’s trust account after redemptions, $201 million from a private investment in public equity (PIPE) led by Foxconn, and a $100 million funding round closed after the SPAC announcement.

Agility had previously projected more than $620 million in proceeds if no shareholders redeemed.

Digit logs operating time, earns revenue

Agility Robotics, which spun out of Oregon State University in 2015, makes the Digit humanoid, which has been moving totes in warehouses. The company claimed that Digit has already logged more than 65,000 hours of operation across nine customer facilities. Customers include AGCO, GXO Logistics, Schaeffler, Mercado Libre, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada.

Agility reported $1.78 million in revenue in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, with a net loss of $138.1 million. About 64% of that revenue came from related parties. The company ended 2025 with $103 million in cash.

The legged robot developer said it has more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders for its next-generation Digit 5, subject to contractual milestones and product specifications. It expects to begin Digit 5 deliveries to early-access customers in 2027.

“Congratulations to the entire Agility Robotics team on this incredible milestone,” said Nicolaus Radford, co-founder and CEO of humanoid startup Persona AI. “At a time when robotics headlines are too often dominated by hype and flashy demonstrations, Agility has focused on the hard work of putting robots to work. Built on a decade of engineering breakthroughs, relentless persistence and real-world deployments, Jonathan and his team have helped turn the promise of humanoid robotics into a commercial reality, and the entire industry should be celebrating.”

Agility said it the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public. But it’s not clear how long that designation will last. The Robot Report broke the news about Agility exploring wheel-based robots in September 2026, and Johnson talked more about it in the company overview (see video above).

“We’re exploring other form factors better suited to work in more consumer-facing domains,” she said. “And whether that means a wheeled base or smaller bipedal form factor, our engineers build the best solutions for wherever hard work is done.”

Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer at Agility, recently said during a social media “Ask Me Anything” that Digit likely won’t get wheels. However, the company is exploring wheeled robots as part of a broader family of multipurpose, human-centric robots.

“Digit likely won’t get wheels. But wheeled robots are absolutely in our exploratory roadmap for a family of robots that focus on being human-centric and multi-purpose,” Hurst said.

From left to right, Cassie, and Digit through the years. | Source: Agility Robotics

Agility Robotics explores licensing its IP

Johnson also suggested that Agility Robotics could license its intellectual property to other humanoid developers, positioning the company as a potential technology supplier to the broader industry. New robots and a licensing strategy potentially open up new revenue paths for the company.

“We envision Agility becoming the backbone of the humanoid industry as the category begins to scale into new markets and use cases,” said Johnson. “Humanoids of all types and builds could benefit from our extensive research and innovation.”

“To build a billion-dollar robotics industry, you need robots that people trust enough to work alongside,” said FORT Robotics founder and CEO Samuel Reeves. “Agility understood early that safety isn’t just a box to check. It’s foundational. Their IPO is a win for Agility and a powerful signal that safety and commercial success go hand in hand.”

The post Agility Robotics begins trading on Nasdaq appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Robotics Startup Radar 2026
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The 2026 Startup Radar presents innovative young companies developing hardware, software, and business models for the next generation of commercial robotics.

The post Robotics Startup Radar 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Robot Report tracks startups throughout the year, and our second annual Startup Radar spotlights some of the most interesting new companies developing commercial robotics and related technologies. From industrial automation and drones to humanoid robots, 2026 has been a year of innovation in the face of persistent labor shortages and geopolitical challenges.

To qualify, organizations must be no more than five years old and must be working on enabling technologies, new full systems, or novel business approaches. The free download notes their application, headcount, and total funding raised to date.

This year, we received a significant number of submissions around software, which is no surprise given the recent wave of interest and investment in data, simulation, and next-generation AI models. They promise to make robots more autonomous, combining the ability to perceive, understand, act, and improve.

The 2026 Robotics Startup Radar features 60 companies working to serve a range of industries, from manufacturing and supply chain/warehousing to agriculture, defense, healthcare, and more. They are based in more than a dozen countries, and several have already successfully raised millions of dollars.

What makes a successful robotics, automation, and AI startup? Such companies offer a strong technical foundation, teams with vision and experience, some business savvy, and key partnerships with industry stakeholders. While not every startup will scale or have an exit or an acquisition, understanding the target market is a key first step.

The Robot Report will continue to cover and share financial news and success stories from this competitive space. As startups look to incubators and grants for support, investors and analysts are always looking for the next big thing and the right mix of technologies to continue expanding automation worldwide.

Note that the call for The Robot Report (TRR) 50 Robotics Innovation Awards, to be presented at the Robotics Summit & Expo in Boston on June 2 and 3, 2027, is already open.

item.title: How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
When designing the robot, GlobalLogic said it didn't want to just quickly design a robot for one use case or environment. 

The post How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
GlobalLogic developed the UV disinfection robot with Haystack Robotics. | Source: GlobalLogic

In hospitals, hygiene is critical. But the cleaning process, which is time-intensive and difficult to scale, remains manual work. This often means the process is also inconsistent. Healthcare facilities are under pressure to care for more patients with fewer resources. These challenges are why the Silicon & Embedded division at GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics engineer a mobile robot to handle disinfection.

The project started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when disinfection became a critical use case for robots.

“Obviously, this was a big use case at that point of time, in terms of being able to sanitize hospitals and care facilities,” Kunaal Mahanti, physical AI lead at GlobalLogic, told The Robot Report. “So [Haystack] came up with this concept of being able to do disinfection better.”

“While there were disinfections which are happening manually, it wasn’t really good coverage,” he added. “We were really the engineering and collaboration partner there to see how we can take this concept and make it.”

The result is an autonomous mobile robot (AMR) that combines real-time perception, edge-based intelligence, and navigation to deliver hospital-grade UV disinfection with minimal human intervention. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company said it can operate safety alongside people, interpret its surroundings, and adapt to changes in its environment.

GlobalLogic aims to create a scalable platform

When designing its robot, Mahanti said GlobalLogic didn’t want to just quickly design a system for one use case or environment.

“We wanted to make it an expandable platform,” he explained. “The idea was that you can look at, for example, the track part of it, which is the thing that is carrying the robot, independent of what it is carrying, which is the UV. Architecturally, you keep them separated so that we can mount other things at a later date.”

“It went from a concept to what would be an architectural foundation, so that it’s not just that one product,” said Mahanti. “It actually becomes a class of solutions that we can build for the same industry segment.”

While GlobalLogic hasn’t done many other deployments in hospitals, Mahanti did say the company used some of the base components of the UV robot for other projects.

“When you look at the platform that moves, there are things that have come out from there in terms of the control of the motors,” he said. “Then we use ROS to do the programming and the sensor fusion part, that is reusable, and we’ve used that. So, if not necessarily the same device, but that architecture broadly.”

Navigating the challenges that come with hospitals

Healthcare facilities are crowded, chaotic, and involve many closed-off spaces, making them difficult for robots to work in.

“The known part was that, obviously, you have to interact with humans. The unknown part is that there are doors, there are things that need to be opened, and you can’t always just barge in,” Mahanti said.

This is different from more common use cases for mobile robots in warehousing or manufacturing, which typically involve open-spaces that are easy to navigate

“There are two modes that we ended up building for [the robots],” noted Mahanti. “Essentially, one was this autonomous mode, where it would navigate and find the right room. The other was a ‘follow me’ mode, in which case it would follow a caregiver or a nurse.”

This means the caregiver can open doors and ensure spaces are ready for the robot to enter. It also means a patient wouldn’t be blindsided by a robot entering their room, for example.

However, designing an AMR that can work in these complex spaces has created benefits in other parts of GlobalLogic’s business. With a much higher bar for safety, the company could apply the platform to other industries.

“The other learning is just being able to be in an environment where you cannot be loud, for example, when we are designing the motors or looking at what we need to put in [the robot],” said Mahanti. “Those things are specific to this industry, but then dealing with that has helped us build machines with higher fidelity elsewhere, where it is not necessarily a given, but it’s a good thing to have. Why wouldn’t you want to have a nice quiet thing that doesn’t interfere with the rest of the environment?”

What’s holding back robotic adoption in hospitals?

While more robots are making their way into hospitals, most people cannot yet walk into their local hospitals and find robots roaming the halls. This is still an emerging area for robotics, so what challenges still exist? Mahanti said three things come to mind.

The first is cost. “There needs to be an ROI,” he replied. “For example, if you look at this use case during COVID, at that point of time, you needed less people in the hospitals. You needed to be safe. It was a big issue. So that ROI was justifiable.”

Second is compliance with medical standards, which becomes much trickier when deploying robots that will interact with the public and patients.

Third is the perception of robots. Mahanti acknowledged that hospital staffers don’t want a big, bulky robot taking up space in busy corridors and elevators.

Prem Balasubramanian, chief technology officer of GlobalLogic, said that safely integrating into hospital workflows is also challenging.

“There are clearly safety concerns, from multiple angles. Navigating in a very human-crowded situation is not easy,” he said. “For a disinfectant use case, if a robot waits for people to keep moving and then slowly moves, you’re okay. But if you’re using it for anything else, like if a doctor calls and you have to get something fast to help a patient or bring some stuff, a robot could get stuck because it sees people moving and it can’t move.”

The hospital is difficult on its own, and it’s made even more difficult when you consider how made-for-humans they are, said Balasubramanian. For example, a robot might be able to navigate an emergency room in a perfect condition with no obstacles, but the addition of patients who constantly moving or being moved and staffers running around to solve critical issues make navigation much more challenging.

“The entire workflow within a hospital is built for humans. You can’t just fit a robot in thinking it’s a human. So, there is work to be done in converting some of the workflow, the spaces, everything,” Balasubramanian said.

item.title: LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action
item.dc:creator: Sponsored Content
item.description:
LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation.

The post LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation. In an evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6, it achieved 36.0% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those target tasks. The model combines large-scale human video, glove-recorded hand motion and embodiment alignment to transfer human manipulation experience to robots.

Liber-0 achieves 36.0% overall success in a zero-shot evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6.

LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a world action model (WAM) pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. The Beijing-based startup said the model combines human video with glove-recorded motion and embodiment-conditioned learning to transfer human manipulation experience to robots.

A central test of Liber-0’s generalization is whether it can perform target tasks without robot demonstrations collected specifically for them. LiberAI evaluated the model on a separate suite of 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks, distinct from its internal scaling benchmarks: 20 pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, 20 non-PnP manipulation tasks, and 20 challenging non-PnP and long-horizon tasks.

Examples from the suite include placing a pen in a pencil case, pushing a drawer closed, and a longer sequence in which a pen is placed in a pouch and the pouch is stored in a drawer.

LiberAI reported task success rates of 63.5% on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on non-pick-and-place manipulation tasks and 10.5% on challenging non-pick-and-place and long-horizon tasks, with an overall success rate of 36.0% across 600 trials.

Here, zero-shot means the evaluated checkpoint was not trained on robot demonstrations collected specifically for these target tasks; pretraining still included robot data.

Why learn from people?

Robot manipulation has traditionally relied heavily on demonstrations recorded on a specific robot for a specific task, usually by a human operator teleoperating the machine. That data closely matches deployment, but collecting it can be slow and expensive, particularly when new tasks or robot platforms require additional demonstrations. Human activity is far more abundant, and much of it is already on video.

The obstacle, according to LiberAI, is that human video does not translate directly into robot commands. Cameras sit in different places, hand poses estimated from video are noisy, and human bodies move differently from robots.

Liber-0 connects human experience with robot action in three ways. First, LiberSense Glove, LiberAI’s data-collection system, directly records hand movements, helping link human video to the motions behind it. Second, LiberAI’s robot platform uses camera views and hand, wrist and waist movements that more closely match those of humans, making skills easier to transfer. Third, a Unified Embodiment Representation gives the model information about body shape and joint movement, so it can adapt actions to the body performing them.

Liber-0 jointly predicts future video frames and actions. This lets it learn from ordinary videos without action labels alongside glove and robot recordings that include measured motion.

Human-to-robot transfer. Conceptual illustration of how action-grounded human recordings and visual and kinematic alignment support transfer to LEO.

Learning actions that robot data lacked

Glove data can also introduce behaviors missing from a policy’s robot data. LiberAI trained policies whose robot demonstrations covered only pick-and-place, while glove demonstrations included actions such as folding, pressing and opening. Performance was measured as a progress score, a 0 to 100 measure that credits partial completion, across four pick-and-place and six non-PnP tasks. With robot data alone, the non-PnP progress score was 2.2. Adding glove recordings of those actions raised it to 47.5, and to 54.6 when the glove set also included pick-and-place, close to the 56.3 scored by a policy trained on robot demonstrations of every action. This controlled experiment is separate from the 60-task suite: the actions appeared in the glove demonstrations but not in the policies’ robot demonstrations.

A quarter of the robot data

A separate experiment examines whether glove recordings can reduce the need for robot demonstrations. In an eight-task evaluation on LiberAI’s robot platform, where the full robot and glove pools contained equal numbers of demonstrations, a policy trained on 25% of the robot pool plus 100% of the glove pool reached a progress score of 75.6. A policy trained on 100% of the robot pool scored 72.8.

In that setting, glove recordings delivered comparable performance with 75% fewer robot demonstrations. The saving applies to robot demonstrations specifically, as the mixed policy still drew on the full glove pool. Because glove collection does not require a robot at each site, LiberAI says experience can be gathered from more people, in more places, and potentially at lower cost.

Evaluating the pretrained model directly

On LiberAI’s internal benchmarks, the pretrained checkpoint achieved progress scores of 81.4 on pick-and-place and 72.3 on non-PnP tasks when evaluated directly. Robot post-training added 2.2 and 1.5 points, to 83.6 and 73.8. LiberAI said the small gain indicates the pretrained model already captures much of the capability needed for the evaluated tasks.

LiberAI has developed an interactive simulation in which users can upload their own objects and watch Liber-0 manipulate them in a virtual environment. The simulation demonstrates object-level generalization: that version of the model was post-trained on 100 hours of simulated teleoperation data and receives no further object-specific training.

“Human video shows what people do, but not exactly how their hands move or how that movement fits a different body,” said Songming Liu, founder and CEO of LiberAI. “Grounding that experience in measured motion and aligning it with the robot’s body is what turns it into robot capability.”

Introducing Liber-0, our World Action Model for zero-shot robot manipulation—including dexterous, multi-step tasks.

Across 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6 and 600 trials, Liber-0 achieved 36% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those tasks:
• Pick-and-place: 63.5%
• Other manipulation tasks: 34.0%
• Challenging multi-step tasks: 10.5%

Zero-shot capability extends beyond individual actions to coordinated sequences.

Pretrained on 2.2M+ hours of human experience, Liber-0 jointly predicts future observations and actions to turn human experience into robot skills.

Technical blog: https://t.co/X5NMTjsr8r

— LiberAI (@liberai_robot) November 4, 2026

What’s next for LiberAI

LiberAI noted that LiberSense Glove currently records hand poses and trajectories but not contact or force, which matter for insertion, fastening and handling soft materials. Tactile and force sensing, alongside data collection across a wider range of homes, remain future research directions.

Watch Liber-0 in action and explore the full evaluation on LiberAI. For collaboration on models, robotics, LiberSense Glove or other opportunities, contact the LiberAI team via the website.
